articles.title: Wildlife conservation cash targets ex-colliery sites
articles.summary: The project aims to create and restore habitats for amphibians and lizards at sites in Yorkshire.
articles.content:
Ponds are to be restored and freshwater habitats created for amphibians and reptiles at two former colliery sites in South Yorkshire.

The Froglife charity has been awarded nearly £890,000 of Lottery cash to carry out the work in Rother Valley, as well as at sites in North and West Yorkshire.

Kiveton and Dinnington Community Woodlands were originally regenerated through the National Coalfields Programme after the pits there closed in the 1990s.

Sheila Grundry, from Froglife, said staff were "delighted" to work in the area because "freshwater will make a lasting difference for frogs and other wildlife and it's a great way for local people to learn new skills".

The £889,761 investment in Froglife's Coalface to Wildspace project will also help local communities connect with nature, according to the charity.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a significant conservation project funded by nearly £890,000 to restore freshwater habitats for amphibians and reptiles at multiple former colliery sites in Yorkshire. This has broad environmental benefits by improving biodiversity and ecosystem health, while also engaging local communities and providing educational opportunities. The project has clear substance and scope, with tangible positive impact on wildlife and people.
articles.personality_title: Nearly £890,000 funded to restore wildlife habitats at old Yorkshire coal sites
articles.personality_presentation:

**What happened** – The charity Froglife received almost £890,000 from the National Lottery to restore ponds and create freshwater habitats for frogs, toads, newts, and lizards. The work will take place at two former coal mining sites in South Yorkshire, including Kiveton and Dinnington Community Woodlands, as well as other locations in North and West Yorkshire.

**Impact** – This project will help amphibians and reptiles by providing better homes and clean water, which are essential for their survival. It also offers local people a chance to learn new skills and connect with nature, making the community stronger and more involved in protecting the environment.

**What's next step** – Froglife will begin the restoration work soon, focusing on building ponds and improving the land to support wildlife. The charity plans to involve local volunteers and teach them about conservation, helping the positive effects last long into the future.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A major investment is restoring old coal mining areas in Yorkshire to create safe, healthy habitats for amphibians and reptiles while engaging local communities in nature conservation.

articles.title: What are heat pumps and how much do they cost?
articles.summary: The government wants more homes to have heat pumps to cut fossil fuel use and drive down energy bills.
articles.content:
Developers will have to install heat pumps and solar panels in all new homes in England under regulations announced in March.

The changes are estimated to add £10,000 to the price of new homes, though owners will likely save money on energy bills over the long term.

In January, the government introduced a £15bn Warm Homes Plan to help UK households pay for green technologies as part of efforts to reduce fossil fuel use and energy bills.

But the autumn budget cut £1bn from the programme to pay for defence.

Heating homes accounts for about a fifth of the UK's planet-warming emissions, so switching from gas and oil to heat pumps is seen as a key way to help meet net zero targets.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on government regulations requiring heat pumps and solar panels in new homes to reduce fossil fuel use and emissions, contributing significantly to climate action and energy savings for households. This policy has broad societal impact and clear environmental benefits, with sufficient context on costs and government support.

**Impact** – Adding heat pumps and solar panels could make new homes cost about £10,000 more. However, over time, homeowners should save money because these systems lower energy bills. **One-sentence takeaway** – New rules in England require heat pumps and solar panels in all new homes to reduce pollution and save energy costs over time.

articles.title: Wading bird called Phil tracked in epic migration to Siberia and back
articles.summary: A bird has astonished conservationists by completing a 6,800-mile round trip to Siberia and back.
articles.content:
Scientists say Phil's extraordinary travels highlight the importance of protecting the world's wetlands, which are havens for millions of migratory birds each year.

Dr Nigel Clark, of the conservation charity, The Wash Wader Research Group, said The Wash is the UK's single most important coastal wetland for migratory waders, with spectacular numbers seen in autumn and winter.

"Tracking birds like Phil the Godwit shows us how connected the Wash is with the rest of the flyway," he said.

Jeff Kew, RSPB Coastal Advisor, said many migratory bird species cross borders, depending on a whole network of wetlands along the way.

That's why it's so important to look after these special places."

Bar-tailed godwits are wading birds of similar size to pigeons, but with long bills and legs.

They are regarded as one of nature's long-distance endurance athletes, with one subspecies making the longest known non-stop migration of any bird, flying 8,425 miles (13,559km) from Alaska to New Zealand.

Phil's journey included a handful of stops to rest and refuel.

He will now spend the winter relaxing with thousands of other wading birds at the Snettisham Nature Reserve in Norfolk.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights a remarkable migratory journey of a bird named Phil, underscoring the importance of protecting vital wetlands that support millions of migratory birds. This has broad environmental significance, emphasizing conservation efforts and the interconnectedness of ecosystems across borders.

articles.title: Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist
articles.summary: A surprising new study suggests Antarctica's towering ice cliffs may be less vulnerable to catastrophic collapse than scientists once feared. After tracking more than 15,000 ice cliffs, researchers discovered that even the tallest cliffs, which can collapse at alarming speeds, often stabilize rather than triggering an unstoppable chain reaction. Underwater ridges, surrounding water, and broken ice appear to provide natural defenses against further collapse.
articles.content:
As temperatures rise, the floating ice shelves that help hold Antarctica's massive ice sheet in place are melting and breaking apart at record rates. As these protective barriers disappear, they expose towering walls of solid ice. Whether these cliffs remain standing or collapse could play a major role in Antarctica's future ice loss and its contribution to rising sea levels worldwide.

For years, scientists have believed that ice cliffs become unstable once they exceed 100 meters in height, roughly as tall as the Statue of Liberty. According to this theory, a cliff that grows too tall will collapse under its own weight, exposing an even taller wall of ice farther inland. That new cliff would then collapse, potentially setting off a chain reaction that causes the ice sheet to retreat rapidly.

But new research from MIT and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) challenges this long-standing assumption. The findings suggest that the fate of an Antarctic ice cliff depends on much more than its height, and that even dramatic collapses do not necessarily lead to an unstoppable retreat.

Published in the journal Science, the study examined satellite observations of more than 15,000 Antarctic ice cliffs collected over four years. Researchers discovered a surprising pattern: When the cliffs collapsed, they sometimes retreated much faster than existing models predicted. Yet rather than continuing to disintegrate, the affected glaciers soon stabilized.

"We found that when the cliffs were retreating, they were doing so faster than what has been modeled, which would mean more ice loss and higher contributions of sea level rise," says study author Caroline Needell, a graduate student in the MIT-WHOI Joint Program. "But because we found that the retreat was short-lived, and all the glaciers eventually stabilized, that would suggest that things won't be so bad. We don't see this runaway effect."

The study's co-authors are Catherine Walker, an assistant scientist at WHOI, and Jeremy Bassis, an associate professor at the University of Michigan.

Why Scientists Expected Antarctica's Ice Cliffs to Collapse

The possibility of runaway ice cliff collapse is described by a theory called marine ice cliff instability (MICI). It proposes that when an exposed ice wall reaches a critical height, its own weight makes it structurally unstable. If the cliff falls and reveals an even taller wall behind it, the process could repeat, progressively eating away at the Antarctic ice sheet.

Earlier research investigated this possibility primarily through computer models. Scientists used the physical properties of ice to estimate how enormous frozen cliffs should behave, then compared those calculations with a limited number of observations from Antarctica. These studies suggested that cliffs taller than approximately 100 meters were particularly vulnerable to collapse.

"Predictive ice-sheet models that have been used so far to represent ice cliff instability just take into account cliff height," Needell notes. "That's the only variable that matters. And once the cliff height reaches the critical threshold, usually 100 meters, it should initiate this runaway effect of ice sheet retreat."

Needell and her colleagues wanted to test those predictions against a much larger collection of real-world measurements. They sought to determine how tall Antarctica's ice cliffs actually become and whether their collapse consistently triggers the destructive chain reactions predicted by existing models.

Satellites Reveal Surprising Ice Cliff Stability

To investigate, the researchers turned to NASA's Ice, Cloud, and Land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2). This spacecraft repeatedly travels over Earth's polar regions, using a laser-based instrument called an altimeter to measure elevations with great precision. Its observations track the heights of glaciers, ice sheets, and sea ice, as well as ocean levels in and around Antarctica.

The team analyzed measurements gathered between 2019 and 2023, examining more than 15,000 ice cliffs at three-month intervals. Most were far shorter than the height considered dangerous by earlier models. The average cliff stood approximately 30 meters tall, although a small number exceeded the proposed 100-meter instability threshold.

The researchers also searched for characteristics that might explain why some cliffs remained stable while others retreated.

One important clue came from the broken ice accumulating in front of the cliffs. Known as mélange, this material consists of a slushy mixture of sea ice and fragments of icebergs. Cliffs that remained relatively stationary tended to have thicker accumulations of mélange, suggesting that the debris could help support the towering ice walls.

"We measured mélange height and found taller cliffs have thicker mélange, which could be a built-in stabilizing effect," Needell explains.

Surrounding seawater provided another possible source of stability. The observations indicated that deeper water can exert greater supporting pressure against an ice cliff, helping counteract the forces that might otherwise cause it to collapse.

Together, these findings suggest that the stability of Antarctica's ice cliffs cannot be predicted by height alone. Conditions in the water surrounding the ice may also determine whether a cliff remains standing.

Antarctica's Tallest Ice Cliffs Collapse, Then Stabilize

"After we did that global analysis, we thought, ok, let's zoom in on the tallest cliffs and see how they're behaving," Needell says.

The researchers selected four locations around Antarctica where satellites had recorded some of the tallest ice cliffs. Each stood approximately 100 meters high, with the tallest reaching 127 meters. The team then reconstructed how these cliffs changed at three-month intervals throughout the four-year study.

The results initially appeared to support the idea that extremely tall cliffs are unstable. These towering walls did collapse, and the glaciers behind them retreated at speeds substantially greater than those anticipated by existing MICI models.

However, the retreat did not continue indefinitely.

"But that retreat was short-lived," Needell notes.

Instead of retreating farther inland in a continuous series of collapses, the glaciers stabilized and eventually advanced outward toward the ocean again.

"It's this rapid retreat, punctuated by periods of stabilization," Needell says. "That was puzzling to us. Then, we thought: We need to look at all the things that affect cliff height."

The unexpected pattern suggested that some overlooked physical processes were interrupting the collapse before it could develop into a sustained chain reaction.

Hidden Ridges Beneath the Ice Act as Natural Speed Bumps

To understand what was stopping the retreat, the team examined the shape of the land beneath Antarctica's ice sheet.

This underlying terrain, known as bed topography, can strongly influence the height and stability of the ice above it. When the ground is relatively flat, the visible slope of the ice more closely reflects the thickness of the ice itself. But when the terrain rises into a ridge or bump, the ice resting on that elevated ground is thinner than its overall surface elevation might suggest.

These buried rises can function like natural speed bumps. By reducing the thickness of the overlying ice, they can make exposed cliffs shorter and less vulnerable to collapse.

When the scientists compared the locations of stabilizing ice cliffs with measurements of Antarctica's underlying terrain, they found that the cliffs frequently stopped retreating where the ground rose beneath them.

The researchers identified another important process. Taller cliffs tended to "thin out" more rapidly as they collapsed. Rather than remaining towering, unstable walls, they could quickly shrink into shorter cliffs that were better able to withstand further collapse.

These effects help explain why the researchers observed rapid initial ice loss followed by periods of stability, rather than the continuous retreat anticipated by earlier models.

What the Discovery Means for Future Sea Level Rise

The findings could help scientists improve predictions of how Antarctica's ice sheet will respond to continued warming.

Although the researchers observed some cliffs collapsing faster than expected, the rapid retreat was temporary in the locations they studied. This challenges the assumption that crossing a particular height threshold inevitably leads to runaway collapse.

The results do not mean Antarctica's ice sheet is safe from further losses. Instead, they reveal that predicting its future requires accounting for several interacting factors, including the shape of the land beneath the ice, the rate at which ice becomes thinner, the depth of surrounding water, and the stabilizing effects of broken ice.

"Now we know what to look for," Needell says. "We really need to know the bed topography, and we need to know the ice thinning rate, in order to get ice cliff instability right, because this value really matters in the context of projecting sea level rise."

By incorporating these additional processes into ice sheet models, scientists may be able to produce more reliable estimates of Antarctica's future contribution to global sea level rise.

The research received partial support from NASA, the U.S. National Science Foundation, and the DOMINOS project, which is part of the International Thwaites Glacier Collaboration.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery that challenges previous assumptions about the stability of Antarctica's ice cliffs, suggesting that catastrophic collapse may be less likely than feared. This finding has broad implications for predicting future sea level rise, a critical global environmental issue. The study is based on extensive satellite data and provides detailed insights into natural stabilizing factors, offering hope for more accurate climate models and better-informed climate action.
articles.personality_title: New study finds Antarctica’s ice cliffs collapse less than expected thanks to natural protections

They found that while some tall cliffs did collapse rapidly, many soon stopped retreating and stabilized instead of causing a continuous collapse.

articles.personality_title_fr: Une nouvelle étude montre que les falaises de glace en Antarctique s’effondrent moins que prévu grâce à des protections naturelles
articles.personality_presentation_fr:

Les scientifiques craignaient que ces falaises s’effondrent les unes après les autres, provoquant une perte de glace rapide et une montée rapide du niveau des mers.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs du MIT et de l’Institut océanographique Woods Hole ont étudié plus de 15 000 falaises de glace antarctiques grâce à des données satellites de 2019 à 2023. Ils ont découvert que, bien que certaines falaises très hautes se soient effondrées rapidement, beaucoup se sont rapidement stabilisées au lieu de continuer à reculer.

**Impact** – Cette étude remet en question l’idée que les falaises de plus de 100 mètres déclenchent toujours un effondrement incontrôlable. L’équipe a trouvé que des éléments comme des crêtes sous-marines, la pression de l’eau environnante et la glace brisée appelée mélange soutiennent les falaises et ralentissent leur effondrement. Cela rend la prédiction de la perte de glace en Antarctique plus complexe mais aussi plus optimiste.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques vont améliorer les modèles des calottes glaciaires en tenant compte de la forme du terrain sous la glace et de la présence de mélange. Cela aidera à mieux prévoir le comportement futur de la glace antarctique et l’élévation du niveau des mers.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les hautes falaises de glace de l’Antarctique sont moins susceptibles de s’effondrer de façon incontrôlable car des caractéristiques naturelles du terrain et de la glace les stabilisent, modifiant ainsi nos prévisions de la montée du niveau des mers.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevo estudio revela que los acantilados de hielo en la Antártida colapsan menos de lo esperado gracias a protecciones naturales
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las plataformas de hielo de la Antártida se están derritiendo más rápido debido al calentamiento, dejando al descubierto altos acantilados de hielo. Los científicos temían que estos acantilados se derrumbaran uno tras otro, causando una rápida pérdida de hielo y aumento del nivel del mar.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores del MIT y del Instituto Oceanográfico Woods Hole estudiaron más de 15,000 acantilados de hielo en la Antártida con datos satelitales de 2019 a 2023. Encontraron que, aunque algunos acantilados muy altos colapsaron rápidamente, muchos se estabilizaron pronto en lugar de seguir retrocediendo.

**Impacto** – Este estudio cuestiona la idea de que los acantilados más altos de 100 metros siempre provocan un colapso descontrolado. El equipo descubrió que características como crestas submarinas, la presión del agua alrededor y el hielo roto llamado mélange ayudan a sostener los acantilados y frenan su colapso. Esto hace que predecir la pérdida de hielo en la Antártida sea más complejo pero también más alentador.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos mejorarán los modelos de las capas de hielo incluyendo la forma del terreno bajo el hielo y la presencia de mélange. Esto ayudará a predecir mejor cómo se comportará el hielo en el futuro y cuánto subirá el nivel del mar.

**Frase clave** – Los altos acantilados de hielo en la Antártida son menos propensos a colapsar sin control porque características naturales del terreno y del hielo los estabilizan, cambiando cómo predecimos la futura subida del nivel del mar.
